title: Recent developments in multi-row cuts
contribution: An Optima survey that organises the 2007-2009 multi-row cut theory as a ladder of relaxations of the simplex tableau (group, continuous-nonbasic, bounded, S-constrained, integer-lifted), reviews closure and split-rank strength results and Espinoza's computations, and names cut selection and density as the practical obstacles.
problem_entry: Single-constraint relaxations are the standard because general MIPs lack structure; multi-row relaxations promise more; the question is which relaxation is both analysable and strong (p. 2).
key_idea: A ladder of relaxations: corner -> data-independent master group -> drop integrality of the nonbasics (lattice-free sets via intersection cuts) -> add back bounds, constraints on the basics (S-free sets), integer nonbasics (lifting/fill-in), with strength judged by closures and split rank (pp. 2-7).
assumptions: Integer-infeasible tableau, f rational non-integral, rational columns, finite support; S = integer points of a rational polyhedron with full-dimensional hull for the S-free results; clean theorems need the all-columns 'data independent' model (pp. 2-6).
proof_devices: Review only: intersection-cut coefficient formula (5), p. 4
Gomory-Johnson minimality conditions (Theorem 2.1), p. 3
Closure comparison via scaled sets alpha*Q: triangle/quadrilateral closures within factor 2 of the hull, split closure arbitrarily bad (Theorem 4.12), p. 7
Dey-Louveaux finite split rank iff not a type-1 triangle (Theorem 4.15) and Dey's log2(l) split-rank lower bound, p. 7
experiments: None by the authors; reports Espinoza: CPLEX 10.2 callbacks at the root, m = 2..15, 87 MIPLIB 3.0/2003 instances, 31% geometric speed-up on solved instances, negative cases acknowledged (p. 7).
positioning: Presents multi-row work as revisiting 40-year-old results of Gomory, Balas and Gomory-Johnson; scope restricted to group-relaxation-based approaches; own papers cited neutrally among others (pp. 2-7).
writing: Theorem-by-theorem tutorial driven by one toy MIP (Cook-Kannan-Schrijver, p. 4); hedged evaluation ('at least theoretically', 'may hold some potential', p. 7); open questions split theoretical/practical (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Open: lattice-free sets in dimension >= 3, how many relaxations can be revoked while keeping complete characterisations; practical: cut selection (O(m^2) row pairs times shapes) and dense cuts hurting other branch-and-cut components (pp. 7-8). The discussion column (pp. 8-10) is Cornuejols, Weismantel and Wolsey's voice.

method_links.note: The 'art lies in obtaining a relaxation' sentence and the MILP relaxation ladder are the toolkit Method 3 later exports to QCQP; Heuristic 4 also gets evidence from the named obstacles cut selection and density (p. 8).
Data independence is already a criterion, but for choosing the model (all-columns master/infinite relaxation), not a measure.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax, then add back one constraint at a time
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The survey is organised as dropping integrality of the nonbasics and nonnegativity of the basics, then reintroducing bounds, constraints on the basics and integer nonbasics one at a time, asking which characterisation survives; the open question asks how many relaxations can be revoked.

transferable: Lay out a relaxation ladder (what is dropped, what is re-added) and attach to each rung the theorem that holds there (pp. 2-6).
Compare cut families by the factor alpha by which their closure can exceed the convex hull, an instance-independent yardstick (p. 7).
Use one toy instance that separates two cut families (finite versus infinite convergence) as the running motivation (p. 4).
Quantify the practical obstacle when listing open questions (O(m^2) row choices times shapes), p. 8.

quotes.text: Another practical difficulty with this class of cutting planes is that they tend to be dense.
Later when Santanu Dey came to Core, my main concern was how to deal with integer non-basic variables, which again led him far beyond what was initially asked.

title: Two row mixed-integer cuts via lifting
contribution: Lifts integer nonbasic variables into two-row lattice-free (split/triangle/quadrilateral) cuts by the trivial fill-in function, proving it is the unique extreme lifting exactly for splits and type-1/type-2 triangles, not for type-3 triangles and quadrilaterals, and giving a sufficient condition for a general fill-in after partial exact lifting.
problem_entry: Single-row group cuts other than GMIC disappointed computationally and GMIC's strength is attributed to its continuous coefficients; new two-row results characterise only the continuous model, so integer nonbasics must be lifted in to obtain two-row analogues of GMIC (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Read GMIC as relax -> extreme in the continuous variables -> lift the integers, and do the lifting step for two rows with the fill-in phi(u) = inf{pi(w): P(w)=u}, keeping pi fixed; minimal iff the fractional parts of D(pi) cover I^2, then unique (Theorems 2-5, pp. 8-10).
assumptions: Mixed-integer infinite group problem MI(I^2,R^2,r); f in the interior of the maximal lattice-free set (boundary case set aside, p. 6); real instead of rational continuous columns as a minor technical assumption handled in Appendix 1 (p. 5); bounded sets for most results (pp. 14-15).
proof_devices: Infinite symmetry check replaced by a covering test: (phi,pi) minimal iff fractional parts of the parallelogram region D(pi) cover I^2 (Def. 6, Props. 5 and 7), pp. 15-18
Finite evaluation of the fill-in by bounding integer shifts (Prop. 3), p. 14
Unimodular normalisation to standard triangles (Props. 8, 9, 13), pp. 19-21
Area of D(pi) affine in f, maximised at vertices; area < 1 implies non-covering and non-minimality (Props. 12, 14), pp. 21-23
Explicit piecewise upper bound function shown to satisfy symmetry and subadditivity, hence equal to the general fill-in (proof of Theorem 5), pp. 27-29
Unique minimal lifting plus extreme pi gives extreme pair (Corollary 1), pp. 18-19
experiments: None ('Computational experiments are under way', p. 29); worked Example 1 runs the recipe on an explicit two-row instance (pp. 11-13); Example 2 shows two distinct extreme liftings for a type-3 triangle (pp. 23-24).
positioning: Chooses the group-relaxation route among three derivations of GMI/MIR/split cuts (p. 2); builds on Gomory-Johnson, Johnson, ALWW, Borozan-Cornuejols, Cornuejols-Margot (pp. 2-3); credits fill-in to Gomory-Johnson and links it to Balas-Jeroslow strengthening (p. 14).
writing: All results stated first in section 3 'The Principal Results', proofs deferred to sections 4-7 (pp. 3, 8-11); practical remarks after theorems (p. 9); a one-row figure motivates the design (p. 7).
limits_future: Only a very special set of inequalities, yet their number is huge and selection is open; future: lifting for type-3 triangles and quadrilaterals, bounds on integer variables, closed forms of fill-in, higher dimensions (p. 29).

method_links.note: Iff characterisation (Theorem 2), positive class (Theorem 3) paired with negative class (Theorem 4) and an explicit non-uniqueness example (Example 2).
Same move as Method 3 (copy the structure of a successful lower-dimensional object into a harder class), but within MILP: one-row GMIC to two rows.
Starts from an empirical regularity (GMIC best single-row cut) and hypothesises its cause, but uses the hypothesis as a design rule rather than proving a proxy theorem.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax, then add back one constraint at a time
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Integer nonbasic variables, dropped to obtain the lattice-free model, are added back by lifting while the continuous part is kept fixed.

transferable: When one cut dominates in practice, name the property that explains it and design the higher-dimensional object to keep that property (pp. 2, 8).
Turn an infinite pointwise check into a covering condition on a geometric region, then use area to show where covering fails (pp. 15-23).
Normalise by unimodular transformations to a few standard shapes before casework (pp. 19-21).
To prove an infimum-defined function minimal, build an explicit upper bound satisfying the minimality conditions (pp. 27-29).
Pair each characterisation theorem with a computed small example that walks through the cut-generation steps (pp. 11-13).

quotes.text: One possible explanation for this is the fact that the GMIC has the strongest coefficients for the continuous variables among all single row group inequalities.
As GMIC is known to be an effective single row general cut, this suggests trying to mimic the above property in the construction of inequalities for two row group problems.

title: Constrained infinite group relaxations of MIPs
contribution: Extends the lattice-free characterisation of minimal and extreme inequalities to the continuous infinite group relaxation with the basic variables restricted to S = P cap Z^m, via maximal S-free convex sets: unique minimal function per set, finite-infinite extremality equivalence, a facet bound 2^m - t via a new notion of order, and a classification of extreme cases in R^2.
problem_entry: The continuous group relaxation drops nonnegativity of the basics although in practice they are nonnegative but unbounded; asks which lattice-free results survive with x in S, as four numbered questions mapped to sections (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Replace lattice-free by maximal S-free convex sets and build pi_K as the support function of a subset of the polar of K - f (a disjunctive cut, can take negative values); introduce the order of K w.r.t. a formulation to bound facets by 2^m - t and classify extreme cases in R^2 (pp. 6-16).
assumptions: S = integer points of a rational polyhedron with full-dimensional hull; W = R^m, no integer nonbasics, no bounds (pp. 2, 4); polyhedrality of maximal S-free sets proved under technical conditions later removed by Basu et al. (pp. 2, 5, 22); K cap conv(S) bounded w.l.o.g. (p. 15).
proof_devices: Polar/support-function construction and separation argument for P(pi_K) = K (Construction 3.1, Prop. 3.2), pp. 6-7
Finite generator set T and finite-infinite extremality equivalence (Prop. 3.6), p. 8
Extremality via linear independence of tight points, with a determinant check (Props. 5.2, 5.4, 5.8), pp. 15-18
Add hyperplanes one at a time to turn an S-free set into a lattice-free set, giving the facet bound (Lemma 4.3, Prop. 4.4), pp. 12-13
Non-extremality by perturbing a facet in two directions so the cut is a midpoint, pp. 15, 17
Compactness (Heine-Borel) argument for polyhedrality following Lovasz (Props. 6.3-6.4), pp. 20-22
experiments: n/a; Example 1.2 gives an explicit facet 3y1 - 0.5y2 + 0.5y3 + 1.5y4 >= 1 of a small MIP (p. 3).
positioning: Extends ALWW, Borozan-Cornuejols, Cornuejols-Margot, Zambelli (pp. 1-2); credits Johnson for the finite-S case and a similar construction and presents its result as the converse (pp. 3, 6); credits Basu et al. for the general version (pp. 2, 5); thanks colleagues for corrections (p. 19).
writing: Intro as numbered questions mapped to sections (p. 2); one example front-loads all new phenomena with forward references (pp. 3-4); explicit version note that the general result was verified by others since submission (p. 2); referee's observation credited in the text (p. 16).
limits_future: Integer nonbasics (G nonempty) not handled though almost all practical instances have them; a Balas-Jeroslow-monoid lifting is sketched but needs a MIP that may not be efficiently solvable; open when it is efficient and strongest (p. 19).

method_links.note: Iff classification by facet count and order; an order-2 two-facet set shown unable to give an extreme inequality.
Redoes Johnson's finite-S facet theory in modern lattice-free language, but within MILP.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax, then add back one constraint at a time
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constraints on the basic variables, dropped by the group relaxation, are added back and the paper asks which lattice-free results survive.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove on the all-columns infinite model, then transfer to finite
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Extremality for the infinite relaxation is shown equivalent to extremality on a finite set of generator columns.

transferable: Open a theory paper with the list of questions the known theory raises for the new model, one per section (p. 2).
Define an integer invariant interpolating between the known and the new case and let it carry the generalised bound (pp. 10-13).
Reduce extremality on an infinite model to a finite set of generator columns and use linear independence of tight points (pp. 8, 15-18).
Prove non-extremality by perturbing the defining set in two opposite directions (pp. 15, 17).
State in the intro which results were since generalised by others (p. 2).

quotes.text: Since the original submission of this paper, Basu et al. [7] have verified that the above result is true in general without requiring any technical conditions.
The referee made the following very important observation.

title: On the extreme inequalities of infinite group problems
contribution: Gives a continuity-free Interval Lemma and a Continuity Theorem that prove for the first time that discontinuous functions can be extreme for pure-integer infinite group problems, relates finite-group facets and infinite-group extremality, gives conditions for limits of extreme functions to be extreme, and proves that extreme functions of mixed-integer infinite group problems are always continuous.
problem_entry: All proven extreme functions were continuous; known discontinuous minimal functions had unknown status because existing tools need continuity; finite-infinite relations were open (pp. 1, 4).
key_idea: Replace continuity in the Interval Lemma by nonnegativity via Aczel's Cauchy-equation result, then show parts of a convex combination inherit continuity wherever phi is continuous, reducing extremality to classical tools (Corollary 1, Theorem 2, pp. 6-8).
assumptions: Pure-integer infinite group problem on the torus with a modulo-1 metric (pp. 3, 5); piecewise linear phi with positive slope at 0 (p. 7); Theorem 7 needs finite subgroups containing breakpoints (pp. 13-14); kappa extreme only for r < 1/3 (p. 18).
proof_devices: Functional-equation (Aczel) variant of the Interval Lemma without continuity (Prop. 2, Corollary 1), p. 6
Subadditivity squeeze: an equality for the average forces it for both parts (eq. (2), p. 7; eq. (12), p. 16)
Agreement on a dense family of subgroups plus continuity gives identity (Theorem 6), p. 10
Counterexample: limit of extreme functions not extreme (Example 2), then diagnosis of which condition of Theorem 7 fails, pp. 11-14
Two-dimensional extension phi(x,y) = pi(P(x+y)) (Prop. 6), p. 22
Continuity of mixed-integer extreme functions via bounded directional derivatives and subadditivity (Lemmas 1-2, Theorem 13), pp. 24-25
experiments: No MIP experiments; merit index computed for the psi_p family (convex in p, largest at the discontinuous limit, Fig. 8, p. 21); the general pattern is observed but 'difficult to prove in general' (p. 20); shooting experiment noted as unusable for discontinuous functions (p. 20).
positioning: Builds on Gomory-Johnson and Johnson and settles the status of Letchford-Lodi, Dash-Gunluk and Richard-Li-Miller functions (pp. 1-4); new families hedged with 'To the best of our knowledge' (pp. 10, 16).
writing: Abstract claims firsts and surprise (pp. 1-2); tools presented as reusable and general (p. 25); each tool followed by an example of use (pp. 10-11).
limits_future: Pure versus mixed structural difference stressed (p. 25); merit-index monotonicity along limits unproved (p. 20); piecewise linearity of continuous extreme functions left open (p. 4).

method_links.note: Counterexample (limit not extreme) paired with sufficient conditions and a diagnosis of the failure; pure versus mixed boundary result.
A strength proxy (merit index) is computed over a family and recorded as an observation, not a theorem; no ground-truth optimum.

Extremality and merit index used as cut-strength yardsticks (citing an empirical correlation); the later doubt about facetness is not yet present. Heuristic 9 also gets evidence: Aczel's functional equations borrowed (p. 6).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove on the all-columns infinite model, then transfer to finite
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Facets of finite group problems on a dense sequence of subgroups give extreme infinite-group functions, and the infinite model is used to settle finite questions.

transferable: Replace a continuity hypothesis by nonnegativity via Cauchy-equation results (p. 6).
Prove a heredity lemma (parts of a convex combination inherit regularity) so classical tools apply to non-regular objects (pp. 7-8).
Build objects as limits of known good ones, show by counterexample that limits can fail, then give sufficient conditions and diagnose the counterexample against them (pp. 11-14).
coauthors: Jean-Philippe P. Richard, Yanjun Li, Lisa A. Miller

quotes.text: Surprisingly, we prove that the functions defining extreme inequalities for infinite group relaxations of mixed integer programs are continuous.
Further, most of the tools used in the past to prove that functions are extreme are not suitable to study these discontinuous functions.

title: The split closure of a strictly convex body
contribution: Proves that the split closure of a bounded strictly convex set with rational affine hull is defined by finitely many split disjunctions (so conic-quadratic representability is preserved), gives a closed-form conic quadratic split cut for ellipsoids, and shows by an ellipsoid in R^3 that the split closure need not be polyhedral.
problem_entry: MILP closure theorems (CG and split closures of rational polyhedra are polyhedra; CG closure of strictly convex bodies is a polytope) prompt the question for split closures, restated as finiteness of the disjunctions needed (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Sandwich SC(C) inside the polytope CGC(C); its boundary points on bd(C) are integral and its interior vertices have epsilon-balls, which only finitely many thin splits can cut (Theorem 1.3, Lemma 2.5, pp. 2-4); plus closed-form ellipsoid split cut and a non-polyhedral example (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: Bounded strictly convex set with rational affine hull (p. 2); reduced to full dimension by Hermite normal form (p. 4); intersection with rational polyhedra not covered (p. 8).
proof_devices: Nested closures SC within CGC within C (Lemma 2.4), p. 3
Thin-split ball lemma (Lemma 2.5), p. 4
Hermite normal form and integer Farkas lemma to reduce to the full-dimensional case, p. 4
Planar case analysis: at most two nontrivial split cuts per disjunction in R^2, hence polyhedral (Lemma 3.1, Corollary 3.2), p. 5
Counterexample certified by a computer check over a provably finite list of splits, p. 7
Convexity/concavity argument for the closed-form ellipsoid split cut (Lemma 3.6, Appendix A), pp. 6, 9-10
experiments: n/a as numerical experiments; one computer-assisted proof step: splits with norm at most 1/0.34 checked by a simple Mathematica program (p. 7).
positioning: Extends Cook-Kannan-Schrijver and later polyhedrality proofs; builds on the authors' CG-closure paper; motivates closed forms without auxiliary variables by cutting-plane efficiency, citing Saxena-Bonami-Lee and Atamturk-Narayanan (pp. 2-3).
writing: Short note; abstract gives the positive and negative result in one sentence (p. 1); remark on the weakest condition the proof needs (p. 4); referee credited for suggesting Corollary 3.2 (p. 8).
limits_future: Extension to strictly convex sets intersected with rational polyhedra needs a set T with two properties whose existence 'remains an open question'; some strictly convex sets have no polyhedral approximation with the same split closure (p. 8).

method_links.note: A MILP closure theorem is carried to convex nonlinear integer sets and representability (SOC) is asked, as in Method 3 step 1's list.
Positive finiteness theorem bounded by polyhedral in R^2 versus non-polyhedral in R^3, and a named open extension.
Computation used inside a proof: a finite candidate list checked by computer to complete the counterexample.

transferable: When moving a polyhedral theorem to convex sets, restate what it really says (finitely many disjunctions) so it can survive outside polyhedra (p. 2).
Prove finiteness of an infinite cut family by sandwiching it inside a closure known to be finite and showing only finitely many members can cut the remaining points (p. 4).
Close a counterexample by proving that only finitely many candidates matter, then checking them by computer (p. 7).
Give closed-form cuts in the original variable space when a lifted representation needs auxiliary variables (p. 6).

quotes.text: In this note, we show that the split closure of a strictly convex body is defined by a finite number of split disjunctions, but is not necessarily polyhedral.
Aided by Lemma 3.6 and Lemma 3.3 we tested this finite list of split cuts using a simple Mathematica [10] program
